TOTALS CROSS-CHECK vs. the document's own Scope-and-Sequence table (printed page 22): final counts are 30 Content Standards / 31 Learning Outcomes / 80 Learning Indicators, against the table's stated grand totals of 30 CS / 30 LO / 80 LI. CS and LI match exactly. LO is one higher than the table states -- this is NOT introduced by the Year Three 'DESIGN FOR LIFE' work done in this pass (that added exactly 3 LOs -- 3.3.1.LO.1, 3.3.2.LO.1, 3.3.3.LO.1 -- matching the table's per-substrand expectation precisely). The extra LO was traced to a pre-existing part of the file: Strand 2 'AESTHETICS AND CRITICISM' > Sub-Strand 'THE WORLD AROUND US', Year Two/SHS 2, which carries 3 Learning Outcomes (2.2.1.LO.1, LO.2, LO.3). Direct re-extraction of that section's source pages (printed ~76-84) confirms all 3 LOs are genuinely printed in the document; the Scope-and-Sequence summary table itself therefore appears to undercount by one for that Sub-Strand/Year (a plausible source table error, similar in kind to the confirmed 'Nations Core Values' typo elsewhere). Not corrected per extraction rules -- flagging here rather than altering the pre-existing Strand 2 content, which was out of scope for this pass.

IN PROGRESS (historical, retained for provenance): incremental full extraction, written strand-by-strand per task instructions to survive session/rate-limit interruptions. This note block will be finalised once all 3 Strands are complete.

Page/pdfPageIndex methodology: two separate pdftotext passes were used. (1) 'pdftotext -layout' was used for the Learning Outcomes / 21st Century Skills / GESI-SEL-National-Core-Values table, because -layout mode preserves left-right column correspondence at the row level for that table (the three columns are of roughly matched height per Learning Outcome). (2) plain 'pdftotext' (NO -layout) was used for the Content Standards / Learning Indicators-and-Pedagogical-Exemplars / Assessment table and the Teaching and Learning Materials rows, because without -layout, pdftotext emits each visual column as one contiguous block (whole Content Standard column, then whole Learning Indicators+Exemplars column, then whole Assessment column) rather than interleaving fragments line-by-line -- this reads far more cleanly for that particular table, whose columns are very unequal in length. Both modes were run against the full 139-page PDF once each; page attribution for every node uses a 'footer-after' rule: a node's page = the printed footer page number (format 'N | ART AND DESIGN FOUNDATION' or 'ART AND DESIGN FOUNDATION | N') of the NEXT such footer line encountered after that node's own code/heading in whichever extraction stream it was read from. pdfPageIndex = printed footer page + 1 (confirmed by direct cross-check of raw PDF page boundaries against footer text at multiple sampled points from page 21 through the final content page 136; the cover page itself, pdfPageIndex 1, is a documented anomaly per the prior inventory pass and is not part of the curriculum tree).

STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE FROM SIBLING DOCUMENT (Art and Design Studio): in this document, 'Teaching and Learning Materials' is printed once PER CONTENT STANDARD (immediately after that Content Standard's last Learning Indicator/Assessment), not once per Sub-Strand. This extraction therefore attaches teachingLearningMaterials as an array on each Content Standard object (field 'teachingLearningMaterials', plus 'teachingLearningResourcesHeaderSeen': "Teaching and Learning Materials"), rather than on the Sub-Strand object as in the canonical schema's Physics-derived example / the Art and Design Studio sibling file. No Sub-Strand-level TLR field is populated for this subject.

GENUINE CONTENT DUPLICATION (Year 1, Strand 1, Sub-Strand 1 'ART ACROSS TIME'): Learning Outcome 1.1.1.LO.3's printed description text ('Analyse indigenous Ghanaian artworks in terms of materials and methods, and their socio-cultural contexts for creative expression in art and design.') is verbatim-identical to 1.1.1.LO.1's description, even though its accompanying 21st Century Skills / GESI / SEL guidance is distinct, unique content (about digital/visual literacy and emerging art traditions) that does not match LO.1's guidance. This appears to be a copy-paste error in the source (the Learning Outcome text cell for LO.3 was not updated), verified by cross-referencing the 'as learners ...' restatement clause embedded at the end of each Learning Outcome's SEL text, which for LO.3 also restates the LO.1 wording rather than LO.3-specific wording. Preserved verbatim, not corrected. Flagged NEEDS_REVIEW on 1.1.1.LO.3.

Reconstruction method for Learning Outcome guidance text spanning a page break: several Learning Outcomes' 21st-Century-Skills/GESI/SEL/National-Core-Values guidance overflows the visual row height of the LO table and continues on the next printed page, where linear text extraction places the continuation at the point in the stream corresponding to its column position on the new page -- which can visually coincide with the START of the NEXT Learning Outcome's own table row. Continuations were reattached to their correct Learning Outcome using the 'as learners <restates the LO's own description text>' clause that consistently closes each LO's SEL paragraph as an unambiguous back-reference. Where this could not be resolved with confidence, the affected node is flagged NEEDS_REVIEW rather than guessed.

learningOutcomes.description: Analyse indigenous Ghanaian artworks in terms of materials and methods, and their socio-cultural contexts for creative expression in art and design.

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication and Collaboration: Learners enhance their ability to communicate effectively, and verbally on indigenous Ghanaian art periods and work to the history of Art of Ghana. Learners enhance their collaborative skills in discursive analyses in oral and/or written descriptions of myths and legends in major indigenous African cultures and their artworks. The use of various search engines and other digital sources as tools for teaching and learning go a long way to improving learner digital competencies. Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: Learners enhance their understanding of how to analyse and determine how materials in the environment are used as basic media in the creation of indigenous art forms. Learners acquire skills to evaluate the impact of indigenous artworks on African cultures. Communication and Collaboration/Global and Responsible Citizenship: Learners improve competencies in oral and written analyses on the impact of indigenous artworks on other cultures. This activity, also, enhances their ability to assess intercultural relationships

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Literacy Confidence Building: The use of Talk for Learning (TfL) interactive processes in groups will foster the development of appropriate register for describing and talking about modern art and its movements and allow learners to talk confidently about art and design works. Glocal Citizenship and Digital Literacy: As learners work in groups, using video presentations to explain Modern Art in relation to historical/current global issues, they acquire digital literacy and glocal citizenship. The generation of timeline infographics showing the various stages and art movements in Western Modern Art from 1850 to 1950 will inculcate digital literacy in the learner. The use of videos and photos of Modern Art Movements promotes digital literacy among learners. The use of computers and projectors for class presentations further enhance learners' digital literacy. Critical Thinking: As learners use videos and photographs to compare the impact of modern art and African art on each other, they enhance their critical thinking abilities. Critical thinking and problem solving: Working in groups to investigate the various channels through which Western Modern Art came to Africa provides opportunity for learners to engage in critical thinking to unearth how various forms of art and design can be introduced into the society. Generating presentation on the channels of influence of Western Modern art in Africa will facilitate critical thinking and problem-solving skills in learners. All forms of investigation involve critical thinking skills to unearth new ideas and concepts. As learners work together to unravel cross cultural influences from modern African artists and works, they invariably develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Communication and Collaboration: Preparation for group presentation in class equips learners with communication and collaborative skills as learners work together for the success of the group. Using brainstorming and other interactive processes and working in groups to share their ideas with peers on popular modern Ghanaian artworks and their uses sharpens the communication and collaborative skills of learners. Cross-cultural Collaboration: As learners from different cultural backgrounds investigate cross-cultural influences from modern African artists and artworks to do group presentations, they discover interrelatedness of cultures, and this helps develop the skill of cross-cultural collaboration among learners. Anticipatory Competence and Innovation: Annotated digital/manual photo/visual diary of images and other forms of mind maps of artworks in Western Modern Art from 1850 to 1950 helps in the formation of artistic mind and innovative thinking. Creativity and Critical Thinking: Analysing Western Modern Art from 1850 to 1950 with relevant resources in relation to materials, imagery, and meaning helps to develop critical minds in the search and utilization of related resources.
